note: Written as a primer for clinicians rather than engineers, and explicit that hallucination and poor generalisation remain blockers to adoption.
title: Large language models in oncology: a review
explain_beginner: Researchers reviewed how artificial intelligence systems that understand and generate human language could help cancer doctors and patients. These systems show promise for helping doctors make decisions, pulling important information from medical records, and supporting patients emotionally. However, major challenges exist before hospitals can safely use them, including the systems sometimes inventing false information and struggling to work reliably across different situations. The authors suggest combining these systems with other technologies to make them more trustworthy and useful in cancer care.
explain_business: This review indicates that while language AI systems could meaningfully support cancer care operations by automating administrative tasks and enhancing clinical workflows, significant technical and safety barriers prevent immediate deployment. Organizations considering adoption should prioritize resolving hallucination and reliability issues before implementation. The recommended approach involves combining language AI with other technologies and implementing rigorous evaluation processes. This positions language AI as a medium-term investment requiring careful validation rather than an immediate operational solution, with success depending on systematic technical improvements and clear governance frameworks.
explain_practitioner: This narrative review surveys large language model applications across three oncology domains: clinician support through decision assistance and automated clinical data extraction, patient-facing tools for information access and psychosocial support, and translational research acceleration. The authors identify critical limitations including hallucination generation, generalization failures, ethical concerns, and integration challenges that currently impede clinical deployment. They recommend embedding LLMs within composite AI architectures to enhance reliability and clinical utility. The review emphasizes that robust evaluation frameworks are necessary before adoption, positioning LLMs as augmentative rather than replacement technologies for oncology practice.
